```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.align = "center"
)
has_gt <- requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(cohortflow)
```

In many studies the rows of the data are not the only units that matter.
Participants sit inside clusters (practices, schools, wards), clusters
inside sites, and repeated measurements inside participants. Reporting
needs counts at more than one level: the CONSORT extension for cluster
trials (Campbell, Elbourne and Altman, *BMJ* 2004;328:702–8) asks for
losses at each stage to be given for clusters *and* for participants.

cohortflow handles this by recording, at every step, how many distinct units
were present at each level you declare.

## Declaring the hierarchy

`cf_hierarchy()` names the levels, from finest to coarsest, and maps each to
the column(s) that identify it:

```{r}
cl <- mock_cluster_rct(n_clusters = 16, n_participants = 600, seed = 7)

h <- cf_hierarchy(
  participant = "participant_id",
  cluster = "cluster_id",
  site = "site_id"
)
h
```

Pass it to `apply_criteria()` with `hierarchy =`. Nothing changes about
which rows are kept; the flow just records the extra counts.

```{r}
crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening", reason = "Failed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent") |>
  group_include(by = "cluster_id", ~ n() >= 20,
                label = "Cluster recruited 20 or more") |>
  randomise(by = "cluster_id", arms = "arm") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent")

flow <- apply_criteria(cl, crit, id = "participant_id", hierarchy = h)
```

## Counts at every level

`levels` in `as_attrition_tibble()` returns one block per level (`NULL`
means all of them):

```{r}
as_attrition_tibble(flow, levels = c("participant", "cluster"))
```

`as_attrition_table()` puts the levels side by side, which is the layout the
CONSORT cluster extension describes. Each criterion reads across both
levels at once:

```{r, eval = has_gt}
as_attrition_table(
  flow,
  levels = c("participant", "cluster"),
  level_labels = c(participant = "Participants", cluster = "Clusters"),
  backend = "gt"
)
```

## How units are counted

Two rules decide when a coarser unit counts as lost. They matter because a
naive count of "distinct clusters among the excluded rows" gives the wrong
answer.

**Row-level steps count from the bottom up.** A cluster is lost at a step
only when its *last* remaining participant is removed there. Losing some of
a cluster's participants is not losing the cluster.

A small example makes this concrete. Cluster A has three participants and
cluster B has two:

```{r}
toy <- data.frame(
  pid = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2"),
  cluster = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B"),
  consented = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
)
toy_flow <- apply_criteria(
  toy,
  cf_criteria() |> include(~ consented, label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent"),
  id = "pid",
  hierarchy = cf_hierarchy(participant = "pid", cluster = "cluster")
)
as_attrition_tibble(toy_flow, levels = NULL)[, c("level", "label", "n", "n_removed")]
```

Three participants were removed (one from A, two from B), but only one
cluster, B, was lost, because A still has participants left.

**Group-level steps count from the top down.** `group_include()` and
`group_exclude()` remove whole clusters, and their participants go with
them. Those participants were not individually excluded, so they are
reported in a separate `n_consequential` column rather than as
`n_removed`. In the trial above, the cluster-size rule removed 5 clusters,
and with them 37 participants who were otherwise eligible:

```{r}
tbl <- as_attrition_tibble(flow, levels = c("participant", "cluster"))
tbl[tbl$label == "Cluster recruited 20 or more",
    c("level", "n", "n_removed", "n_consequential")]
```

This is the distinction the cluster extension draws between losing a
cluster and losing participants.

## Composite levels: stepped-wedge trials

A level can be identified by more than one column. In a stepped-wedge
trial, each cluster contributes a cluster-period for every period of the
roll-out, so the cluster-period is identified by `cluster_id` *and*
`period`:

```{r}
sw <- mock_stepped_wedge(n_clusters = 8, n_participants = 400,
                         n_periods = 4, n_sites = 2, seed = 3)

h_sw <- cf_hierarchy(
  observation = "event_id",
  cluster_period = c("cluster_id", "period"),
  cluster = "cluster_id"
)

crit_sw <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented", reason = "Did not consent") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew") |>
  group_include(by = c("cluster_id", "period"), ~ n() >= 8,
                label = "Cluster-period has 8 or more")

flow_sw <- apply_criteria(sw, crit_sw, id = "event_id", hierarchy = h_sw)
```

```{r, eval = has_gt}
as_attrition_table(
  flow_sw,
  levels = c("observation", "cluster_period", "cluster"),
  level_labels = c("Observations", "Cluster-periods", "Clusters"),
  backend = "gt"
)
```

The cluster-period rule removed 12 cluster-periods but only 3 whole
clusters: the others still had at least one period with enough
participants.

Stepped-wedge results are also often shown by site and period. `group_x` and
`group_y` repeat the attrition table for each combination; see
[Attrition tables](https://mattmoo.github.io/cohortflow/articles/attrition-tables.html#grids-by-site-and-period).

## Characteristics at the cluster level

`as_characteristics_table()` and `stack_cohorts()` take a `level` argument
to describe units at that level rather than rows. Every variable must be
constant within a unit, as cluster-level variables such as site and arm are:

```{r}
as_characteristics_tibble(
  flow,
  vars = c("site_id", "arm"),
  steps = list(0, "Cluster recruited 20 or more"),
  level = "cluster",
  wide = TRUE
)
```

## Limits

- `levels` cannot be combined with `group_x`, `group_y`, `branch_by` or
  `count_by` in the same table.
- `as_consort_diagram()` draws one level at a time: rows by default, or a
  hierarchy level with `count_by` (`count_by = "cluster"` draws a
  cluster-flow diagram). For a cluster trial, draw the participant-level
  diagram and report cluster counts in the attrition table alongside it.
- `cf_hierarchy()` does not require strict nesting, but its counts are
  easiest to read when each level nests in the next.
